comments.author: @OfficialBeeswax
comments.text:
This is one of the many problems with not having single-buyer healthcare. If there were a single-buyer system in the US, it would simply force the air ambulance companies to charge reasonable rates, or it would set up its own service and cut costs down to the absolute minimum.

Also fun fact: here in the Netherlands we only have air ambulances for the islands. What we do have, however, both on the islands and the mainland, is the "trauma helicopter". This is a nationwide network of helicopters that, rather than bring the patient to hospital, bring the hospital to the patient. These trauma helicopters are staffed by an experienced trauma surgeon and an anesthesiologist. They are fully equipped to perform surgery on patients at whatever location. Therefore, if someone is gravely injured, they can be operated on and stabilised at the scene of the accident, and thén be taken to hospital by a regular ambulance. And obviously, this is all covered by the mandatory health insurance we all have.

comments.text: I’m a medevac pilot in the four corners area (fixed wing) and I regularly transfer patients from southern Utah and Colorado. Something people don’t realize is that most air ambulance transfers are not in helicopters but in fixed wing aircraft like PC-12’s and King Airs. We save lives, and try to make money too. The American system isn’t perfect, lots of times I believe that facilities and doctors just want the patient the hell out of their hospital, to better care, so they call us. It’s not all so cut and dry.

comments.author: @EmeraldPencil46
comments.text:
I can thank Ornge for saving my mom’s life last year. She has a sudden, unexpected, and unexpected cardiac emergency where she died at least 3 times. It happened in the middle of cottage country, where it took paramedics half an hour to get out to us, and another half hour to get to the nearest hospital, a hospital which had maybe 20 beds and the most complex machine they had was an xray. 

If it wasn’t for the amazing paramedics, nurses, and doctors, my mom wouldn’t still be alive, and for Ornge and their amazing pilot couple who flew her out to Kingston where she was treated so well. 

And living in Canada, the largest bill we were given wasn’t for the hospital stay, or the air ambulance ride, or any of the follow ups, but the $45 bill for the first ambulance ride. 

And if for whatever reason something terrible happened and me or a loved one, and we need the best hospital we can get, once we’re transported to the nearest hospital and stabilized, there’s a free maybe 20 minute helicopter ride from our home to the 2nd best hospital in the world. And again, the largest bill we’ll see is a $45 ambulance fee.

As an FYI an Air Ambulance rider is available for a lot of insurance. I pay $12 extra a month and it covers ALL air related expenses should I need them. Hopefully I never do but an extra $144 a year is well worth that peace of mind when I'm out on the motorcycle.

Also, the idea that air Ambulances perhaps don't save additional lives is idiotic. I dated a girl who was an Air Nurse. The amount of additional training they received makes EMTs look like school nurses. It's not always about the transportation time to a trauma center; it's about how quickly they can get high-level care to the patient.
